meta.title: Bengali A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Bengali → English (see the Bengali, recall the meaning) and English → Bengali (see an English meaning, recall the Bengali). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for learners of Bengali, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 272 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, introducing yourself, family, numbers, telling the time, days and months, food and drink, shopping and money, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, and the pronouns, question words, postpositions and conjunctions every sentence is built out of — and the other 228 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Bengali, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. The deck teaches the standard colloquial language (cholito bhasha) shared by West Bengal and Bangladesh; where an everyday word differs between the two — জল and পানি for water, নমস্কার and সালাম for a greeting — both are taught. Every headword is printed in the Bengali script with a romanisation beneath it, Wiktionary's own (ô for the open o of the inherent vowel, ō where the o-sign is written, a dot under the retroflex letters, ẏ and ẇ for the glides: kôra, bhalō), so the deck can be studied before the script is fluent; the Bengali Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the script itself. Bengali has no grammatical gender. The 202 nouns show their definite form ('the …', with -টা), their plural and their genitive ('of …'); the 72 verbs show their present, their past and their 'having done' form, where the stem's vowel changes and the irregular verbs show, and behind the All forms fold every tense by person, at the three levels of address — তুই intimate, তুমি familiar, আপনি polite. Real example sentences come with 481 of the 500 words, three apiece for 434 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, forms and romanisation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
